rv.q: While Wilkinson catches the mood and the measure of the city instinctively, the framework of the drama is erratic.
Smith’s performance as Gigi makes Wilkinson’s writing sparkle with humour.
Night City may or may not be a 'choreopoem', but whatever you want to call it, it's a fine piece of new writing and deserves to have a big audience.
Olivia Jamieson’s set, and Arnim Friess’ lighting and video design, are immersive without ever being distracting.
Night City shines a light on the hidden underside of London.
Wilkinson’s script is occasionally poetic, but too many plots are packed into 80 minutes, and Night City’s determination to come up with a resolution, involving an AI bot, seems a little desperate.
While the three main threads don’t exactly coalesce into a fully integrated whole, there is a genuine sense that the playwright has worked to weave them.
The velocity of his stagecraft is exhilarating.
The production has a strong and committed ensemble, creating a vivid portrait of a city that never stops moving.
It rewards attention and offers something fresh to the debate, and some overfamiliar stories.
Night City is bold, energetic and visually inventive, powered by two particularly impressive central performances and exceptional movement work.
Wilkinson is a skilled writer and Night City has sharp and hilarious one liners throughout, but the play felt more complex than it needed to be.
It's worth seeing for the visuals and the fantastic performances, but be warned, the writing struggles to be anything more than wafer thin.
Unfortunately, despite there being plenty to admire within the production, the play didn’t quite resonate with me as much as I had hoped.

Night City paints a picture of an unsustainable work culture and the chains that bind people, but it tries to cover too much in too little time which dilutes the power of what could have been a sharper, more resonant exploration of the gig economy.
This is an energetic and skilfully executed production that vividly captures the pressures of precarious urban life.
Overall, Night City feels messy, with too many characters, short scenes and not enough depth.
It is a hugely impressive play which deserves to fill the Little to the brim for its run – and a longer life somewhere too.
It is this nuanced feeling that is beautifully conveyed in the equally heartbreaking and heartfelt message audiences take away from the show.
Night City gives those people a stage.
There are moments of genius in the writing of some of the characters

Unfortunately, although the individual elements of the show are outstanding, after about ten minutes I found myself wishing someone would simply pull down the chains, turn on the lights and make everyone fully visible and the story easier to follow.

cn.t: Critics find this gig economy drama well-intentioned but overstuffed, praising strong performances and timely subject matter while noting the plot crams in too many dramatic incidents. The fast-paced production resonates emotionally despite sometimes muddled storytelling.
